temperance

/TEM-per-uhns/ - the stress falls on TEM · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Temperance means moderation in action or thought.

Their debate coach preached temperance with evidence: two strong studies, she said, beat ten shaky ones read aloud in a hurry.

Example

The village praised old Toma's temperance every harvest: he sold only what the cellar couldn't hold, kept seed corn no matter the price, and never borrowed against a season that hadn't happened yet.

Temperance is moderation practiced as a principle—not one refused dessert but a settled habit of stopping at enough. The word once headlined campaigns against alcohol, but its reach is wider: spending, speech, ambition, and appetite can all be governed temperately.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

moderation: Moderation is the everyday word for keeping to sensible amounts—of food, spending, screen time. Temperance is moderation promoted to a principle: a settled, deliberate policy of stopping at enough, kept up over years. You can eat in moderation this week; temperance is the standing rule behind every week.

self-restraint: Self-restraint is the act of holding yourself back, moment by moment—swallowing the retort, skipping the splurge, each one a separate effort of will. Temperance is what those moments become once they harden into settled habit: the principle rather than the push. Self-restraint is exercised; temperance is lived.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

excess: more than sense allows

overindulgence: treating yourself past the point of good

Where it sits · how far the self-denial reaches

restraint → temperance → abstinence

restraint vs. temperance: Restraint is the milder, moment-sized act beside temperance—declining the second helping tonight says nothing about tomorrow, while temperance is the standing habit of stopping at enough, night after night.

abstinence vs. temperance: Abstinence goes further than temperance or restraint—the abstinent give a thing up entirely, while the temperate keep it, measured to enough.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — temper: to mix in due measure, restrain (Latin temperare)

Suffix — -ance: state or quality of

Put it together: Temper- (to mix in due measure, from Latin temperare) + -ance (state of) = the state of keeping things in measure. A blacksmith tempers steel and a baker tempers chocolate—each a careful mixing toward balance—and temperance applies the same craft to appetite and conduct.

Use the root in a new word: temperate: Gardeners in the temperate zones set out their seedlings weeks before their cousins farther north dare to.

Word Choice

formal / a little old-fashioned

Temperance is moderation elevated to a virtue and practiced as policy—use it for habits and principles, not single acts (one skipped dessert is restraint; a lifetime of small portions is temperance). Its reference-list neighbor measured describes the same spirit in one performance—a measured reply, a measured pace—while temperance is the standing rule behind them.
